title: What would happen if a supervolcano woke up?
subtitle: A volcanic winter
subject: sciences
description: An eruption big enough to fill 400 million Olympic swimming pools would not only devastate its surroundings. Ash across a whole continent, gas high in the atmosphere: the real danger would come from the climate.
author: muhammad-zaheer

hero.hook: The eruption would begin in a single place, but its effects would travel around the planet.

blocks.text: An eruption that throws out more than **1,000 km³** of ash, rock and gas, enough to fill **400 million** Olympic swimming pools: that is the scale of a [[supervolcano]]. It does not necessarily look like a cone-shaped mountain. Its giant eruptions leave behind a [[caldera]] instead, a huge basin formed when the ground collapses after a large amount of magma escapes from below.

The danger would not stop at the foot of the volcano. Ash could cover vast areas. Gases would rise high into the atmosphere. Some effects would be felt thousands of kilometers away, others all around the planet. So what would happen if a supervolcano really woke up?

A supervolcano would not erupt without warning. Before a major eruption, magma, the molten rock buried beneath the ground, starts moving and building pressure. That movement sets off swarms of earthquakes. It can make the ground rise or sink. The mix of volcanic gases changes too. Scientists watch for all of these signs.

For a giant like [[Yellowstone]], in the United States, those warnings could last for weeks, months, perhaps longer. Yet "waking up" does not mean an explosion is certain. It means the volcano is becoming more active, and that it needs to be watched more closely.
A volcano can shake, swell and release more gas, then settle down again without the slightest eruption. Waking up is not the same as blowing up.

If the eruption came, the area around the volcano would be devastated. Yet lava would not be the main threat. The real danger has a name: the [[pyroclastic flow]], a cloud of scorching gas, ash and pieces of rock that races down the slopes at high speed and destroys almost everything in its path.

blocks.caption: A pyroclastic flow races down the side of Mount Mayon, in the Philippines.

blocks.text: A massive column of ash and gas would also rise high above the volcano. And as enormous volumes of material leave the ground below, part of the land above could collapse. Near the eruption, the toll would be catastrophic. But the danger would not end there: hot ash and gases spread quickly, and falling ash would affect a far larger area.

Unlike the ash from a wood fire, [[volcanic ash]] is not soft. It is made of tiny, sharp fragments of rock, minerals and volcanic glass. Even a thin layer causes problems: it damages engines and machinery, contaminates water supplies, cuts visibility and disrupts road and air travel alike.

blocks.caption: The Cougar Point Tuff (Idaho): ash welded into rock by a supereruption of the Yellowstone hotspot.

blocks.text: For an eruption on the scale of Yellowstone, computer models suggest that ash would cover much of North America, reaching more than **1,500 km** from the volcano. The layer would get thinner with distance, but its effects would still be serious very far from the crater. You do not need to live next to a supervolcano to feel the consequences.

A supervolcano would also affect regions far beyond the ash cloud. A giant eruption releases [[sulfur dioxide]], a sharp-smelling gas that can rise very high into the atmosphere. There it forms tiny particles that reflect part of the sunlight back into space. The planet then cools temporarily: this is what is known as a volcanic winter.

blocks.caption: The U.S. naval station at Subic Bay, Philippines, blanketed in ash after the June 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo.

blocks.text: The eruption of [[Mount Pinatubo]], in the Philippines, in **1991** was far smaller. Even so, it lowered the global average temperature by about **0.5°C** for close to two years. A supervolcano would have a stronger effect. But scientists still do not know how much the Earth would cool, or for how long. The biggest impact would probably come neither from lava nor from ash, but from changes in the atmosphere and the climate.

A supervolcano would probably give warning before it blew, devastate its surroundings and bury a continent in ash, but its widest effect would come from the atmosphere: a global cooling whose scale nobody yet knows.
